title: One more evening
told: a story of Saints Benedict and Scholastica

card.from: a story of Saints Benedict and Scholastica
card.keepWhy: Go to the one who understands, and stay a while.
sources: Gregory the Great, Dialogues II.33-34: Scholastica, Benedict’s sister, consecrated to God from childhood, came to see him once a year at a house near the monastery; they spent the day in praise of God and holy talk and at dusk ate together; she begged him to stay the night and talk till morning of the joys of heaven; he refused, saying he could not stay outside the monastery; she laid her joined hands on the table and bowed her head on them; from a clear sky came such thunder, lightning and rain that neither Benedict nor his brothers could set foot outside; “God forgive you, sister, what have you done?” “I asked you, and you would not listen; I asked my Lord, and he heard me”; they spent the whole night in holy talk; “she could do more because she loved more” (illa plus potuit, quae amplius amavit); three days later he saw her soul go up to heaven like a dove, and laid her in the tomb he had prepared for himself.
Luke 1:39-56 (the Visitation: Mary goes with haste to Elizabeth; Elizabeth’s blessing; Mary stays about three months). The Visitation is the second joyful mystery of the rosary; feast 31 May.
Feast of Saint Scholastica, 10 February. The Rule of Saint Benedict.
check: Gregory says only that she was his sister; that she was his twin is later tradition, and the lesson leaves it out.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when you have big news, is there one person you want to tell first?
options: then hold their face in your mind while you watch.
that’s okay. this story is about the one who gets it.
that’s so common. this story might change that.

steps.line: Saint Benedict had a sister, Scholastica, a nun who lived nearby. Once a year she came to see him, and they spent the whole day talking about God.
On one visit, they talked and ate together until night fell. Then Benedict stood up. A monk had to be back in his monastery by night.
Scholastica begged him, “Please stay tonight. Let’s talk until morning about the joys of heaven.” He said no. It was against the rule.

steps.q: Scholastica folds her hands on the table, bows her head and prays. What happens next?
o: Benedict changes his mind on his own
A wild storm breaks, and no one can leave
She gives up and says goodbye
steps.why: A sudden storm, out of a clear sky. Thunder, lightning, rain so heavy no one could step outside.

steps.line: Out of a clear sky, a storm broke: thunder, lightning, pouring rain. No one could step out the door.
“Sister, what have you done?” She smiled. “I asked you, and you wouldn’t listen. So I asked my God, and he listened.” They talked all night.

steps.q: Benedict wrote a famous rule for monks. Why would the storyteller let him lose this argument?
o: Love can weigh more than even a good rule
Even founders of rules need humbling
Scholastica was the holier of the two
steps.why: The rule was good. But that night, love and the need to be together came first, and God sided with love.

steps.line: Three days later, Benedict saw a dove rise toward heaven and knew his sister had died. He laid her in the tomb he had made for himself.

steps.pre: Pope Gregory, who told the story, wrote: she could do more, because she
steps.why: Loved. He was strict about a good rule. She loved more, and love won the night.

steps.q: Benedict laid his sister in the tomb he had made for himself. Where was he buried when he died?
o: In the same tomb, beside her
In the cave at Subiaco where he began
steps.why: Pope Gregory wrote that not even the grave would part two whose minds had always been one in God. At Monte Cassino you can still visit their shared tomb.

say: here’s what i love. scholastica didn’t send a message. she walked to the one person who understood her, and she fought for one more evening with him.

catholics see the same thing in the visitation: mary hurried to elizabeth, and elizabeth blessed her without asking for proof. it’s the second joyful mystery of the rosary. some news is meant for the one who gets it.

steps.q: She asked her brother and he said no. She asked God, and the storm came. What does the story suggest about God?
o: God sides against rules that are too strict
Small, loving wishes matter to God too
Prayer works best once a person has refused you
steps.why: Not a grand miracle for a grand cause. A storm, so a sister could have one more evening with her brother.

today.say: today, go to the one who understands: a visit, a call, a voice note to the person who’d get it without the backstory. stay a little longer than you planned. if you pray, you can thank God for them.
options: lovely. one more evening, in a way.
good. scholastica walked a long way for hers.
